newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO say they keep doors open.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO say they keep doors open.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians said on Tuesday they were keeping the door open to restoring severed contacts, despite a deepening rift following a Tel Aviv suicide attack.
In the Sri Lankan capital of Colombo, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said he was ready to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss peace in the Middle East.
"Why not? If this is for peace I am ready, but if it is for propaganda, it is something different," Arafat told reporters.
In Jerusalem, Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan said the Israeli leader had been willing to meet Arafat. "As far as I know there is nothing planned right now," he added.
Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy appealed to Arafat this week to cut short a trip to Asia and Africa and return to Gaza to deal with the deepening crisis.
U.S. officials said a peace mission by Middle East negotiator Dennis Ross was under consideration but far from set.
On Monday, a top Palestinian security official said he had stopped security coordination with the Israelis.

"We stopped the security coordination as a result of the Israeli contravention of the agreement by establishing settlements," Mohammad Dahlan, head of Preventive Security in Gaza, told a news conference.
Palestinian demonstrators and Israeli troops have fought daily street battles in the West Bank since Netanyahu broke ground last week on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

The Tel Aviv bombing on Friday, which claimed the lives of three Israeli women, further strained relations. An anonymous caller claimed responsibility in the name of the Islamic militant group Hamas in a phone call to Israeli police.
Ending a visit to Sri Lanka, Arafat said his Palestinian Authority had acted against those who opposed the law, including Hamas.
Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser Dore Gold, asked whether there were contacts between the sides, told Reuters: "There may be low level talks on security."
He said high-level contacts could resume if the Palestinians fought terrorism and prevented attacks.
But Arafat also accused Israel of fomenting confrontation between Palestinian groups, saying Israel wanted civil war.

"The Israeli government is looking to having instability and confrontation between the Palestinians, a civil war, which we cannot accept," Arafat said when asked about Israel's demand that he clamp down on militant groups.

Ross, the U.S. Middle East peace envoy, underscored in an interview with the MSNBC cable television network the need "for 100 percent effort" in fighting terrorism and said: "We'd like to see them (the Palestinians) do more."

Arafat, before leaving Sri Lanka for Bangladesh, said: "Peace is an open target. Our target is a comprehensive, lasting peace in the area...We have worked hard for peace and don't forget that the majority of the Israeli people are for peace."
But Bar-Illan complained Arafat wasn't doing enough to ensure security.
"We know for a fact that he hasn't done a thing either before the bombing in Tel Aviv or after," Bar-Illan said.
